newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Zaireans party as Mobutu leaves and Swiss freeze villa.
newsitem.headline: Zaireans party as Mobutu leaves and Swiss freeze villa.

text.p: Zairean rebel representatives celebrated in Geneva on Friday as Zaire said embattled president Mobutu Sese Seko was giving up his powers and Switzerland ordered a freeze on his luxury Swiss villa.

"We're so very happy. We're throwing a little party. Too bad we can't get our Primus beer here," one of the Zaireans, Jose Mutombo-Kady, said after Switzerland announced the freeze in response to a request from the public prosecutor of the rebel-held Zairean city of Lubumbashi to block Mobutu assets.
"We're grateful. Justice has won over politics."
An official statement in Zaire's capital said the 66-year-old veteran strongman, who left Kinshasa on Friday, was giving up his powers.
Ghislain Demofik, another rebel representative, predicted that the president's departure would increase the pressure on other countries to block his assets.
"This is the beginning of a new era. We are sending official requests to the United States, France, Belgium, Austria and Portugal to freeze all of Mobutu's assets," he told Reuters.
Switzerland stopped short of ordering a freeze on any funds Mobutu may have in the Alpine country.
A government statement said the Zairean request to do so did not have sufficient detail on other Mobutu assets and "for the moment, does not allow the possible adoption of other measures".

The statement said federal police and justice authorities asked the canton of Vaud to put the sprawling luxury villa in Savigny near Lausanne on the real estate register as "blocked" and "cannot be transferred until further notice".
Federal police said this was the first time Switzerland ordered a freeze on the property of a ruler still in power.
The Swiss government had ignored a previous demand from rebel leader Laurent Kabila to block Mobutu's assets, saying it had to come from official Zairean authorities to be legitimate.

But the rebels took no chances this time. With the help of a Swiss lawyer, they cunningly presented the Swiss with copies of official documents proving the prosecutor was appointed by Mobutu although he had later switched allegiance to the rebels.
The Swiss statement said he "appears therefore to be a competent representative of the Zairean judicial authorities".
Mobutu is reputedly one of the richest men in the world. His opponents accuse him of getting rich from the misery of the poor in his mineral-rich vast African country.

He has a string of luxury properties including an apartment in Paris, property in Brussels, a south of France holiday home and an estate in the Portuguese Algarve which also houses his vintage wine cellar reputedly with 14,000 bottles.
His Spanish interests reportedly include a luxury villa and hotel in Marbella and a home in Madrid.
Mobutu's villa in Savigny near Lausanne, kept spotless and hidden from prying eyes, has a market value of some $5.5 million, according to Swiss federal police department.

Photographs from the air of the luxury estate, which Mobutu bought for his first wife Marie-Antoinette in 1968, show a huge house, swimming pool, garages, a pond surrounded by trees and a small chalet in the sprawling garden.

Mobutu's bank accounts are less visible. Switzerland's top banking watchdog, the Federal Banking Commission, has ordered an official search for Mobutu accounts among banks and given them until the end of May to report.

If the search finds sizeable accounts of Mobutu, some fear Swiss banks may get caught up in a legal wrangle similar to that surrounding the millions of former Philippines ruler Ferdinand Marcos, now the subject of a long court battle.

The Swiss government is desperately trying to escape from charges of collaboration of its banks with Nazi Germany with its honour and dignity intact and another banking scandal is the last thing it wants.
